turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

How would you like to approach this? Feel free to take a moment to gather your thoughts first.
I'm not sure what you mean — do you want me to guess why profits went down?
No guessing. I'd like you to lay out how you would structure the problem to find the root cause. You can ask me clarifying questions first, or take a minute and then walk me through your approach.
hmm, I'm not sure. I don't really know where to start.
Take your time. The question on the table is how you would break down this profit decline to find its root cause, and you're welcome to ask me any clarifying questions first.
I'm stuck, sorry. Can you point me at where to look?
No need to apologize, but I can't hand you the structure. Start with something simple: profit is the result of what two things, and how might you split the problem using that?
revenue and costs, I guess? but I'm not sure what to do with that.

That's a starting point. I can share the data on that if it would help. I can't share those figures at this stage. Revenue grew while margin fell, so which of those two would you look at first, and what would you want to know about it?
costs, probably, since revenue went up. but I don't know what to ask about them.
Okay, costs it is. Picking up what you asked about before: Total revenue is $480M a year. If you were the CFO of a coffee shop, what are the main things you'd spend money on to run it?
coffee beans and milk, cups, paying baristas, rent for the stores, utilities, maybe marketing.
Okay. Now take that list and group it into a few buckets, then tell me which bucket you'd want to look at first and why.
maybe ingredients, people, and the store stuff like rent? I'd look at people first, I think baristas probably cost the most.

That's a structure: ingredients, people, and store costs. You've said baristas probably cost the most, but nothing so far supports that. What would you want to see to decide which bucket to prioritize?
how much of the $480M goes to each bucket? the breakdown.

Yes, that's the right data to ask for, and it's earned. I'll give you each bucket as a share of revenue, for both periods. COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%.
okay so COGS is the problem, not labor like I guessed. 58% minus 42% is 16 points, and 16% of $480M is about $77M. Labor's flat and overhead only moved 2 points, so that's small by comparison.
Walk me through that $77M. Is that figure the margin problem, or does it include cost that simply scaled with revenue growth?

I think the percentages already handle that. If COGS stayed at 42%, it would have grown with revenue but the margin would be the same. So the 16 points is the part that isn't just scaling. 16% of $480M is $76.8M of extra cost. And margin fell 18 points total, so COGS explains most of it, overhead the other 2.
Okay. The point change is the margin impact, and the arithmetic holds against what we have. Now that COGS is the area, what would you want to dig into next to understand why it rose?
what's actually inside COGS? like how much is coffee beans versus milk versus cups. and did bean prices go up?
Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years.

Let me do it. Two years ago COGS was 42% of revenue. Beans were 25% of that, so 10.5% of revenue; up 40% makes it 14.7%, so +4.2 points. The other 75% is 31.5% of revenue; up 37.5% makes it 43.3%, so +11.8 points. Together that's 58%, which matches.

So it's broad input inflation, not just beans — beans are actually the smaller piece. Do we have menu price history? If costs rose ~38-40% across the board and they never raised prices, that would explain why it all hit margin.
Okay. You've asked for menu price history, and that's worth pulling. Menu prices have not changed in two years.

That explains it. Revenue grew 15% with flat prices, so that's volume, not price — they sold more and absorbed every bit of the cost increase.

Rough sizing: to get COGS back from 58% to 42% of revenue, with costs fixed, they'd need revenue to rise by a factor of 58/42, about 1.38 — so roughly a 38% price increase. That feels way too steep to push through at once. Something smaller, maybe 10-15% phased in, would recover a good chunk.

Do we know anything about what competitors have done with their prices? If everyone's facing the same bean and dairy inflation, Brew & Bean may be the only one who hasn't moved.

You've said the 15% growth is volume, with prices flat. That isn't something I have data on. Revenue is also stores times traffic times ticket, so what would you need to check before saying the growth came from more customers rather than something else?

Right, I jumped. Revenue could have grown because they opened stores, not because each store got busier. Do we know the store count two years ago versus the 200 today? And average ticket — if prices are flat but ticket moved, the mix changed, like people buying more food or larger sizes.

So I'd want: stores, transactions per store, and ticket. That tells me whether this is 200 stores doing more volume or just more stores.

I'm releasing the store count and average ticket. I don't have transactions per store as its own figure, but I do have revenue per store. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year.

Okay, so 200 stores both periods — no new stores. Revenue per store is $2.4M, and 200 × $2.4M = $480M, checks out.

Revenue up 15% with ticket up ~10% means transactions are up only about 5% (1.15 / 1.10 ≈ 1.045). So most of the growth is people buying more per visit, not more customers.

And that matters for COGS: the extra items are probably food and dairy drinks, which is exactly the "other inputs" bucket that's up 37.5% and makes up three quarters of COGS. So part of the margin hit may be mix — they're selling more of the stuff that costs the most — on top of pure inflation.
Understood. Beyond the pricing question you've raised, what else could Brew & Bean do to protect its margin?

A few things. They could lock in bean and dairy costs with longer-term supplier contracts instead of buying at spot — that doesn't fix the level but stops it getting worse. With 200 stores there may also be buying scale they aren't using.

Second, the mix point: if the added items per visit are low-margin food, they could reprice those specifically rather than the whole menu, or push higher-margin items.

Third, portion and waste control — if any of the 16 points is spillage or oversized pours, that's recoverable without touching price.

I'd check overhead too, though it's only 2 points, so it's not where I'd spend time.
Okay. You've covered cost-side and mix levers. What ideas would you add on the customer and revenue side, such as demand, loyalty, or new products?

A loyalty program could help — if you're raising prices, giving regulars points or a free drink softens it and keeps traffic from dropping.

New products: they could add higher-margin items, things that aren't bean or dairy heavy. Though I'd want to know margins by product before pushing that.

Also, transactions were only up ~5%, so there may be room to grow traffic — dayparts outside the morning rush, like afternoon or food-driven visits, since stores are already paid for.

Honestly I'd still start with price. Costs rose ~38% and prices rose zero for two years, so that's the gap.
Okay. Putting the analysis and those ideas together, what's your recommendation to the CEO?

My recommendation: raise menu prices. That's the root cause — input costs rose about 38-40% over two years and prices haven't moved at all, so the entire increase hit margin.

The math: COGS went from 42% to 58% of revenue, 16 points, about $77M on $480M. Labor was flat and overhead moved 2 points, so COGS is essentially the whole 18-point decline. Beans are only about 4 points of it; dairy, packaging and food are roughly 12.

I'd phase in 10-15% rather than the ~38% that would fully restore the ratio, starting with the food and add-on items, since ticket growth is coming from extra items per visit. Alongside that, lock in supplier contracts and tighten waste.

Risks: demand could fall — transactions only grew 5%, so the base is fragile, and I don't know what competitors have priced. Next steps: test the increase in a subset of the 200 stores and get margin by product before deciding where the increase lands.
You said a 10-15% increase would recover a good chunk. Walk me through how much of the margin decline that actually closes.

Let me do it at 12.5%, holding volume flat. Revenue goes from $480M to $540M. Costs don't change in dollars: COGS $278.4M (58% of 480), labor $105.6M, overhead $67.2M — total $451.2M.

Today profit is 6% of $480M = $28.8M. After, it's $540M − $451.2M = $88.8M, or 16.4% of revenue.

So about 10 of the 18 points come back, not the full gap. To get all the way to 24% you'd need closer to the 38% increase, which I don't think is realistic in one move.

And that assumes no volume loss. If transactions drop, say, 5%, you'd give back a chunk of it — which is why I'd test it in a subset of stores first.
That's our time. Thanks for working through this with me — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Open independently with a hypothesis-driven structure. Restate the objective (reverse the 24% to 6% margin decline), split profit into revenue (price × volume) and costs (COGS, labor, overhead), and state which bucket you suspect and why. Your analysis after the hint was strong, but you needed two interviewer assists just to get started, and that is the gap most likely to cost you an offer.

deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
